GAIA

Ground Activity Intelligence & Analysis: NISAR radar maps of ground deformation along the East African Rift

339 granules2 rift mosaics~6% of each file streamedL + S bands
  • Mission: turn satellite radar data into a live, region-wide map of ground movement along the East African Rift, in centimeters
  • Why: the rift drives earthquakes, volcanic activity (Afar) and landslides, and is far too long to watch site by site
  • How: NISAR (NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) sees through cloud and at night; InSAR turns two images into a motion map
  • What we built: an end-to-end pipeline (search, stream, process, mosaic) and a hazard web map, from one earthquake alert to a finished map
  • Team: E.T
Hi, we're team E.T. GAIA stands for Ground Activity Intelligence and Analysis. The East African Rift is slowly pulling Africa apart, which brings earthquakes, volcanic activity in Afar and landslides, over a distance far too long to watch site by site. NISAR is a radar satellite from NASA and ISRO that sees through cloud and at night. We built an end-to-end pipeline that finds the data, streams only what it needs, converts it to centimeters of ground motion and stitches it into rift-wide mosaics, plus a web map for hazard monitoring. The numbers at the bottom are what the rest of the talk explains: 339 granules, two mosaics, about 6 percent of each file streamed, and both radar bands.
The science

A Splitting Continent, Measured From Space

  • The problem: the African plate is splitting along the East African Rift, from Afar to Mozambique, with earthquakes, magma intrusions and landslides
  • InSAR (Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar) compares two radar images of the same ground taken days apart; the phase change is the motion
  • It is measured along the line of sight (LOS) to the satellite: displacement = phase × wavelength / 4π, in centimeters
  • Ascending and descending passes see the ground from opposite sides; together they separate vertical from east-west (plate-opening) motion
  • Pixels with low coherence (signal quality) are masked out, so noise is not drawn as motion

L-band (NASA)

Wavelength about 24 cm (our files: 1.229 GHz = 24.4 cm). Holds its signal over vegetation and long ranges.

S-band (ISRO)

Wavelength about 9 cm. Reacts more strongly to small motions, for finer detail.

GAIA uses both L-band and S-band.

[tile]
One real granule: warm and cool colors are opposite directions of motion along the line of sight
The rift is where Africa is slowly tearing in two. InSAR works by taking the same radar picture twice and comparing them: the phase difference is ground movement along the satellite's line of sight, and the formula is phase times wavelength over four pi, giving centimeters. Pixels with low coherence, meaning a poor signal, are masked so noise is not drawn as motion. A satellite pass going up and one going down view the ground from opposite sides, which lets us separate vertical motion from east-west plate opening. NISAR carries two radars: NASA's L-band at about 24 centimeters, which keeps its signal over vegetation and long distances, and ISRO's S-band at about 9 centimeters, which is more sensitive to small motions. GAIA uses both bands.
The data

339 Granules, 6% of the Bytes

  • Source: NISAR GUNW products (Geocoded UNWrapped interferograms: ready-made ground-motion images) from the Alaska Satellite Facility (ASF)
  • One granule is about 1 GB and covers about 330 × 330 km (roughly 110,000 km²) on an 80 m grid, about 4,200 × 4,100 pixels
  • Search: area 28-45°E, 20°S-15°N, PROVISIONAL maturity, 2026-09-01 to 2026-11-15: ASF returned 1,507 granules

The input is NISAR's GUNW product from the Alaska Satellite Facility: a geocoded unwrapped interferogram, so the hard part of InSAR is already done. One granule is about a gigabyte and covers about 330 by 330 kilometers on an 80 meter grid. We searched the whole rift for the last few months and ASF returned 1,507 granules; we took the latest pass of every track, which is 339: 176 ascending and 163 descending, plus 17 earlier frames to fill holes, so 356 processed. Downloading all of that would be roughly 340 gigabytes. Instead we use HTTP range requests to fetch only the datasets we need, in 4 megabyte blocks with read-ahead and retries. On a tested granule that was 59 megabytes out of 981, about 6 percent, so roughly 20 gigabytes in total.
How it works

The Pipeline, Start to Finish

1Trigger or requestUSGS quake alert or user area + dates
→
2SearchASF API: GUNW, orbit direction, data maturity
→
3Streamrange requests, 4 MB blocks, read-ahead, retries
→
4Processphase to cm, coherence mask, multilook
→
5Mosaiclevel, feather, Web Mercator
→
6Map dashboardLeaflet + Flask, live progress

Start: two ways in

  • • Automatic: reads the live USGS earthquake feed, takes the epicenter, builds the search box and time window, clips nearby faults
  • • Manual: type an area and dates on the dashboard or command line
  • • Both run the same search

Processing and parallelism

  • • Displacement = phase × λ / 4π; color and numeric GeoTIFFs per granule
  • • Granules run in separate processes: the HDF5 library holds a global lock, so threads gave no speed-up
  • • One failed granule never discards the successful ones

Mosaic and map

  • • Latest pass per (direction, track, frame); scale-and-offset leveling matches neighbours, a smooth feathered blend hides seams
  • • Rows resampled to Web Mercator so the overlay lines up on the map
  • • Flask server streams job progress (server-sent events) to the page

Also in the code, not yet used on the rift run

Tropospheric (atmospheric) correction from phase screens in the product · 2D decomposition into vertical + east-west from an ascending and a descending raster · time-series velocity inversion (needs about a year of acquisitions)

The pipeline starts one of two ways. Automatically, it reads the live USGS earthquake feed, takes an epicenter, builds a box of about one degree and a window of about twelve days and clips nearby faults; or a user types in an area and dates. Both run the same search at ASF. Then we stream only what we need and convert phase to centimeters, masking low-coherence pixels and multilooking to reduce noise. Granules run in separate processes because the HDF5 library's global lock stopped threads from running in parallel, and one failure never discards the successes. The mosaic step picks the latest pass of every frame, levels the offset and scale between neighbours, feathers the overlaps and resamples to Web Mercator so the overlay sits exactly on the map. A Flask server connects the map to the pipeline and streams live progress. The code also supports atmospheric correction, vertical and east-west decomposition and time-series velocity; we have not used those on this run yet.
The product

The Interactive Map and Hazard Layers

  • A Leaflet web map (open-source mapping library) shows the rift mosaics: one layer per direction, with an opacity slider and a layer selector
  • Context layers: live USGS earthquakes (circle size = magnitude, color = depth), GEM active-fault traces, plate boundaries and Ethiopia critical infrastructure (15 features)
  • Basemaps (street, satellite, terrain and more) and quick jumps to the rift, Addis Ababa or the world
  • Start from the map: enter an area and dates, watch live progress, and the new overlay appears when the job finishes

Multi-sensor fusion: combines InSAR speed with rainfall + soil moisture (landslides) or earthquake swarms + SO₂ gas (tectonic and volcanic) to cut false alarms into a 0-100 risk score

Inverse-velocity forecasting: when 1/velocity trends to zero, velocity is heading to infinity, which marks the projected failure time

This is where it all comes together. The Leaflet map shows the ascending and descending rift mosaics with an opacity slider, next to live USGS earthquakes sized by magnitude and colored by depth, GEM active faults, plate boundaries and critical infrastructure. You can also start processing from the map and watch progress live. On top, the hazard modules turn deformation into decision support: multi-sensor fusion combines InSAR speed with rainfall and soil moisture for landslides, or earthquake swarms and gas for tectonic and volcanic cases, into a 0 to 100 score with four bands from Green to Evacuate. Inverse-velocity forecasting projects failure time when the inverse of velocity trends to zero. Be clear that these are rule and physics based and demonstration-grade: we estimate deformation, not earthquake probability.
What happened

Results and Problems We Solved

  • Outputs: per-granule ground-motion rasters (numeric cm + color) and two full-rift mosaics, ascending and descending, about 2,400 × 4,100 pixels each
  • Robustness: two granules failed on network errors and succeeded on retry; the overlay is built from whatever succeeded
  • Quality: 80+ automated tests pass; progress bars and ETA for the long runs
  • Honest status: a coverage view built from passes on different days, not a single moment
ProblemFix
Short reads at block edges: “filter returned failure”→Every read returns exactly the bytes asked
Threads blocked by the HDF5 global lock→Separate processes
Output named after a temp file, never found→Temp file carries the real granule name
Progress said “done” after the first granule→Overall progress across all granules
Overlay up to ~30 km off the map→Resample to Web Mercator
Visible seams between frames→Leveling + feathered blend
We processed all 339 granules, 176 ascending and 163 descending, plus 17 earlier-pass frames to fill holes in the mosaic: 356 in total. The outputs are numeric and color ground-motion rasters per granule and two full-rift mosaics. Two granules failed on network errors and succeeded on retry. Along the way we fixed six real problems: short reads at block boundaries that corrupted compressed data, a global lock that stopped threading from helping, output files named after a temp file, a progress bar that said done too early, an overlay up to 30 kilometers off, and visible seams between frames. Looking ahead

Impact, Limits and Next Steps

Impact

  • A repeatable way to turn NISAR data into hazard-ready maps
  • About 6% of the data downloaded, so a whole rift is practical on a laptop
  • One workflow from an earthquake alert to a finished map
  • Supports earthquake, volcano and landslide monitoring

Limits

  • PROVISIONAL-maturity data (early, not final quality)
  • Line-of-sight motion only; one layer at a time on the map
  • A long smooth color gradient is probably an orbital or atmospheric ramp, not removed yet; ionosphere not removed
  • The reference pixel is a heuristic; the map estimates deformation, not earthquake probability

Next steps

  • Combine ascending + descending into vertical and east-west layers for the whole rift
  • Verify the atmospheric correction, remove the ramp and check against independent measurements
  • Run time-series velocity once a year of data exists
  • Fuse L-band and S-band results for finer detail

Application in AI

The maps are analysis-ready data (centimeters, with a signal-quality mask) that can feed predictive models, including the risk-scoring and time-to-failure code already in our project. No model is trained yet: that needs more months of data and labelled events.

Thank you. Questions?
The impact is a repeatable, low-bandwidth route from satellite data to hazard-ready maps. We want to be upfront about limits: the data is still provisional, motion is line-of-sight only, a long smooth color gradient is probably a ramp we have not removed, and we estimate deformation, not earthquake probability. Next we will combine ascending and descending data into vertical and east-west layers, verify the atmospheric correction, run time-series velocity once we have a year of data, and fuse the L-band and S-band results. Because the maps are analysis-ready they can also feed predictive models, but we have not trained one yet; that needs more months of data and labelled events. Thank you, and we're happy to take questions.
